name: Maw
description: Maw is a historic trick-taking card game that was popular in 16th century Britain and Ireland. It is the ancestor of the Irish game Spoil Five and other related games. Played with a distinctive 52-card deck where the 5 and 9 of trumps have special powers, Maw features unique ranking orders and the ability to renege (not follow suit) under specific circumstances.

history.origins: Maw was extremely popular in 16th century Britain, played at the court of James I. It spread to Ireland where it evolved into Spoil Five and related games like Twenty-Five, Forty-Five, and One Hundred and Ten.
timeline: 1580s: Maw first documented in England, played by nobility
1600s: James I of England was known to play Maw
17th Century: Spreads to Ireland and evolves into Spoil Five
18th-19th Century: Regional variants develop throughout Ireland and Britain
Present: Survives as Spoil Five and related games in Irish communities
history.cultural: A game of historical significance, representing the trick-taking tradition that influenced many modern card games. It was considered a game of skill and status in Elizabethan and Jacobean England.
history.evolution: The game's unique features (special 5 and 9, reneging rules) were preserved in its Irish descendants. The name 'Maw' may derive from the Welsh word for 'large' or from the Irish 'MÃ¡il'.

setup.players: 2-10 players (best with 5-7). Can be played individually or in partnerships.
setup.deck: Standard 52-card deck. In trump suits, cards rank: 5 (highest), J, A, K, Q, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 4, 3, 2. In non-trump suits: K (high), Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, A (low).
setup.dealing: 5 cards to each player, dealt in packets. Remaining cards form the stock.
setup.equipment: Standard deck, chips or counters for scoring.

rules.objective: Win at least 3 of the 5 tricks to win the game and collect stakes from opponents.
rules.gameplay: Player to dealer's left leads. Players must follow suit if able. The highest trump or highest card of led suit wins the trick. Winner leads to next trick.
keyRules: 5 of trumps is always highest trump
9 of trumps is second highest trump
Must follow suit unless reneging is permitted
First to win 3 tricks wins the game
Special reneging rules apply with certain cards

strategy.basic: Remember the special ranking in trumps - the 5 and 9 are the most powerful cards. Try to win early tricks to gain the lead.
strategy.intermediate: Use reneging opportunities wisely. Save your 5 and 9 of trumps for critical tricks. Pay attention to which cards have been played.
strategy.advanced: Card counting is essential. Track the trumps that have been played to know when your 5 or 9 will be unbeatable. Understand the complex reneging rules to exploit them.
tips: The 5 of trumps is the most powerful card - save it for a critical trick
Watch for opportunities to renege when opponents lead high cards
If you don't have trumps, try to lose tricks early to conserve high cards
Remember that Aces are low in non-trump suits
